title: Maclaurin Series
body:
A [[Taylor Series]] centred at $a = 0$. That is the entire definition; it gets its own name only
because it is the case that comes up constantly.

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^n
$$

## The five to memorise

Everything else is built from these by substituting, differentiating, integrating, or multiplying,
which is legal inside the radius of convergence (see [[Power Series]]).

| Series | Expansion | Valid for |
|---|---|---|
| $e^x$ | $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{n!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\sin x$ | $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$ | $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n$ | $\vert x\vert < 1$ |
| $\ln(1+x)$ | $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}$ | $-1 < x \le 1$ |

Sine is odd and its series has only odd powers; cosine is even and has only even powers. The
fourth row is just the geometric series from [[Infinite Series]] read backwards, and it is the one
that generates the most others.

Adding the sine and cosine rows with an $i$ attached gives $e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x$, which is
Euler's formula. See [[Polar Form]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], where it is used rather than derived.
